segments.en: Alii. That is how you say hello in Palau, and you will hear it with a big smile. Say it back, and you have already made a friend.

Palau is a scatter of more than three hundred islands in the western Pacific, east of the Philippines. Only a handful are lived on, and many of the rest are wild green domes rising out of turquoise water.
The most famous are the Rock Islands, mushroom-shaped limestone islets covered in jungle. The sea has worn away their bases, so they look as if they are floating on the lagoon.
Hidden among them is Jellyfish Lake, a saltwater lake where countless golden jellyfish drift towards the sunlight each day. Cut off from the sea, they have lost most of their sting.
Underwater, Palau is one of the great diving places of the world, with walls of coral, sea turtles, manta rays and reef sharks gliding through clear blue water.

Palauans care deeply for this ocean. Much of the sea around the islands is protected, and every visitor signs a promise, stamped in their passport, to tread lightly and look after the islands for the children of Palau.
Traditional society here is matrilineal, which means land and family titles pass down through the mother's line. Women hold great respect and play a key role in choosing chiefs.
In the villages you may see a bai, a traditional meeting house with a tall pointed roof. Its beams are carved and painted with stories of legends and village life.
Those stories inspired storyboards, wooden panels carved in the same style, which are now a much loved Palauan art.
People speak Palauan and English. Meals often include taro, which grows in wet fields tended by women, fresh fish, coconut crab and tapioca, and food is always shared at big family gatherings.
Palau's capital is Ngerulmud, a quiet place on the largest island, Babeldaob, while most people live in and around the lively town of Koror.
Old money is still treasured here. Traditional beads and pieces of turtle shell are exchanged at important family occasions, carrying the respect and history of a whole clan.
Before you go, drift in a kayak between the Rock Islands as the evening light turns the water gold. Then look west across the sea, where the islands of the Philippines are waiting.
